Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in three sentences

D'Ieteren's share price pays for its holding wrapper and gives Belron, the world's dominant vehicle-glass repairer, almost for free: the shares trade at about 10x earnings and at a 45 percent discount to a sum of the parts of about EUR 317.

At the guideline fair multiple of 10.29x, the shares return about +20 percent to 31 December 2027, almost all of it from EPS growth of 13 to 15 percent a year that Belron's operations, not financial engineering, now drive.

The Belron listing is an option on top of that earnings return, and the option pays only if D'Ieteren pairs the listing with a channel that passes Belron's value to D'Ieteren's shareholders.

D'Ieteren is, in economic substance, a 50.3 percent stake in Belron. D'Ieteren is a family-controlled Belgian holding. Belron (Safelite, Carglass, Autoglass) supplies about 65 percent of D'Ieteren's forward PBT GS and about 77 percent of its net asset value. Around the Belron stake sit a shrinking Belgian Volkswagen importer (D'Ieteren Automotive), a good French parts distributor (PHE, Parts Holding Europe) and a 40 percent stake in TVH, the leader in forklift spare parts.

The eight things that matter.

1
D'Ieteren's earnings compound at 10 to 11 percent a year, and from FY2027 the growth comes from operations, not from financial engineering. PBT GS rises from EUR 955.6m in FY2025 to EUR 1,266m in FY2028, and EPS from EUR 12.95 to EUR 17.68. Of the EUR 274m rise in PBT GS from FY2026 to FY2028, Belron's operations supply 56 percent, PHE 15 percent, the Automotive floor 14 percent and Belron's lower finance costs only 11 percent. Every broker still calls interest reduction "a primary driver". Interest reduction was the primary driver in FY2026; it is not from FY2027 onward, and I expect the market to recognise in 2027 that operating growth deserves an operating multiple.
2
FY2026 earnings are almost known, FY2027 earnings depend on two drivers, and FY2028 earnings carry a downside tail. H1 2026 is reported (PBT GS +8.4 percent at constant currency), so the FY2026 EPS range is narrow, at EUR 13.45 to 13.85. FY2027 needs Belron's operating result to rise about 9 percent and Automotive to stop falling; the FY2027 EPS range is EUR 14.4 to 16.2, with about a 65 percent probability of landing within 5 percent of the base case. FY2028 adds the risk that US insurers push back on Belron's prices; the FY2028 EPS range is EUR 15.9 to 18.6, skewed down.
3
Belron's growth engine is mechanical and still running: each new windscreen carries more cameras, and more jobs are routed to the operator that can recalibrate them. Recalibration penetration rose from 47.2 percent of jobs (FY2025) to 52.1 percent (H1 2026). Belron's operating margin was 23.0 percent in FY2025 and 24.4 percent in H2 2025; organic growth was 7.3 percent against minus 1 percent at Boyd, the nearest rival. Belron cut net debt from 5.4x to 4.3x EBITDA in eighteen months while paying dividends. The company's target of a margin "above 25 percent by FY2028" is within 60 basis points of the H2 2025 margin already reported.
4
The shares trade at the bottom of their own ten-year valuation range, so the return at the guideline multiple comes from earnings, not from a re-rating. The two-year-forward P/E of 9.6x to 10.0x sits at the 21st to 23rd percentile of the stock's history, which places the stock in the Bottoming phase, with a guideline fair multiple of 10.29x (the 30th percentile). At 10.29x the model's total shareholder return is +20.0 percent to 31 December 2027 (16.9 percent annualised: 15.7 points from earnings, 1.5 from the multiple, 2.6 from dividends) and +31.7 percent to 30 June 2029. Each turn of P/E above the guideline adds about 10 percent to the return; the ten-year median multiple of 11.0x alone adds EUR 14 a share.
5
The catalysts arrive in a dated sequence, and the largest catalyst, the Belron listing, runs on a clock that other shareholders hold. On 10 March 2027, a new chief executive will most likely report an FY2026 result at the top of guidance alongside a cautious FY2027 framing (a scheduled air pocket, about 70 percent likely). In the second quarter of 2027, the sell-side's revision cycle turns. In September 2027, the H1 2027 result tests whether guidance is raised (about 45 percent likely). Between months six and eighteen, Belron's private-equity co-owners, who hold 40 percent and need liquidity, drive the listing. In 2029, Belron's leverage falls below 3x and its dividends to D'Ieteren grow.
6
A Belron listing is necessary but not sufficient to narrow D'Ieteren's holding discount. The precedents split by what each holding did with its event: Investor AB's discount narrowed to 12 percent and Exor re-rated, while Prosus's discount stayed at 40 percent and Kinnevik's widened to 50 percent. A secondary sale by the private-equity owners brings D'Ieteren no cash. What narrows the discount is a channel from Belron's value to D'Ieteren's shareholders, such as Belron distributions or D'Ieteren buybacks, and nobody has promised one.
7
Two negatives are missing from the market's narrative. First, US insurers are re-basing calibration fees and the mark-up over NAGS (National Auto Glass Specifications, the industry's list price) at contract renewals from 2027 to 2029; the evidence says the re-basing will be gradual, and the base case already carries about a third of a 20 percent cut in US calibration prices. Second, the timing of the Automotive restructuring depends on consultation under Belgium's Renault Act, and nobody has published a savings figure.
8
The case is concentrated, and the share price answers to the company's own events. The case rests on one asset (Belron), one customer type (insurers), one price benchmark (NAGS), one junk-rated capital structure with 77 percent floating-rate debt, and one country market (Belgium) for the second driver. Over the last six months, 81 percent of the stock's daily price variance has been its own (beta 0.6 to the sector), so the multiple will respond to D'Ieteren's events, not to a sector recovery.

The risk/reward is skewed to the upside over twelve months. The skew is mildly positive in earnings, because FY2026 should beat and FY2027 should be delivered above its cautious framing. The skew is positive in the multiple, because the 30th-percentile guideline multiple applies to a stock whose operating growth the market is about to recognise as operating. The skew is binary in the Belron event.

1

The operating environment: tailwinds, headwinds and their absence

Key message

The business weather is good and the market weather is bad: the favourable forces sit where D'Ieteren's profit is, and the hostile forces sit in a shrinking Automotive business and in the share price's multiple.

Evidence. The external forces run in opposite directions in D'Ieteren's two largest businesses, and the profit weight is lopsided toward the favourable one. Belron supplied about 57 percent of FY2025 group-share operating profit and supplies about 65 percent from FY2026.

Belron has four tailwinds.

  • Content per windscreen is rising, with two years of visibility. Camera brackets were fitted on 49 percent of windscreens in 2020 and on 60 percent in 2025. The EU's General Safety Regulation 2 mandates windscreen cameras. Each recalibration of a camera adds EUR 150 to 300 to a job. Bernstein's growth algorithm for Belron is 2 percent volume plus 3 to 4 percent from complexity, mix and price.
  • US claims volume is recovering from a cyclical trough. US glass-only claim frequency is 1.5 percent against a five-year average of 2.1 percent, so the headroom for recovery is real. US motor premiums fell 5.1 percent year on year in August 2026, which unwinds the 2022 to 2024 episode in which drivers avoided claims. Belron's North American organic growth was +9.4 percent in H1 2026.
  • A contract adds volume. Safelite has administered State Farm's National Glass Program since July 2025. Competitors expect Safelite's share of State Farm glass jobs to rise from 30 to 40 percent toward 70 to 80 percent.
  • The technical bar is rising and pushing one-person shops out of the market. Each site needs about USD 55,000 of equipment for advanced driver-assistance systems plus USD 18,775 a year of maintenance, and each technician needs 41 hours of training a year.

PHE and TVH have milder tailwinds. PHE benefits from an ageing car parc (12.9 years on average, with the prime six-to-fourteen-year cohort growing 12 percent by 2028) and from share gains against shrinking incumbents: PHE's organic growth was +6.0 percent in H1 2026 against minus 5.1 percent at LKQ Europe and a market near +2 percent, and LKQ's failed German enterprise-software rollout opens a Benelux opportunity. TVH benefits from an industrial recovery, with sales up 7.7 percent at constant currency in H1 2026 on construction demand.

D'Ieteren Automotive faces four structural headwinds. The company itself confirms that the Belgian market has plateaued at 400,000 units a year, 20 percent below pre-pandemic. Chinese entrants took 13 percent of European sales in August 2026, up from under 8 percent, and over 30 percent of untariffed plug-in hybrids. Volkswagen's Future Plan 2030 cuts 50,000 jobs, halves the model range and addresses 500,000 units of European overcapacity. Belgian fiscal change removes electric-vehicle subsidies in 2026, ends 100 percent company-car deductibility for electric vehicles on 1 January 2027 and introduces mobility budgets from 2027, in a market where corporate buyers take 70 to 75 percent of cars. D'Ieteren's Belgian market share fell 153 basis points to 21.5 percent in a year.

Belron also faces three forming headwinds. First, US insurers are starting to regulate calibration billing: State Farm, GEICO and Allstate pay flat rates of USD 390 to 550; State Farm has introduced its ADAS Map documentation tool; Travelers is studying an hourly rate near USD 200 against flat fees of USD 250 to 400; and Liberty Mutual is expected to act within 14 months. Second, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration forecasts a strong El Nino and therefore a mild northern-US winter; the precedent is H1 2024, when Belron's North American organic growth fell to 0.2 percent and its margin fell 80 basis points. Third, US consumer confidence is at the survey's lowest reading.

At the level of the equity, the market environment is hostile. Markets are in a risk-off regime, with the US 10-year yield near 5.1 percent, Brent at USD 111 and French sovereign stress. Car-retail and leasing stocks have de-rated (Inchcape fell 9.3 percent in a day on 22 October), and consumer discretionary is a double underweight in Viewforth's "Fitness for Fighting" sector tilts. Currency is a further swing factor: 55 percent of Belron's revenue is North American and unhedged in translation, so a 5 percent move in EUR/USD moves D'Ieteren's EPS by about EUR 0.27.

Inference and so-what. Profit-weighted, the tailwinds outweigh the headwinds roughly 60 to 40, and the tailwind that matters most, content per windscreen, is mandated, measurable and not yet decelerating. The headwinds are concentrated in a segment whose share of profit is falling from 17 percent to about 7 percent, and in the multiple rather than in the earnings. The forming insurer headwind is the one to respect: insurer pricing changes travel through rolling two-to-three-year contract renewals and reach Belron's margin from 2027. For that reason the base case fades Belron's price and mix contribution from 5.1 percent (FY2025) to 2.5 percent (FY2028).

Counter-case. The recovery in claims volume reverses a trough in consumer behaviour, and the US consumer is weakening just as insurers cut reimbursement to contain claim costs. Premium pressure could again drive drivers to defer repairs or pay cash at independent repairers, where Safelite under-indexes, in 2027. A mild El Nino winter would also land in the half-year that sets the tone for the March 2027 guidance.

What would change my view. A large US carrier moving to a coordinated flat-rate or hourly calibration schedule across its whole book in 2027 (the base case assumes gradual, carrier-by-carrier action); Boyd or Driven Brands reporting a renewed fall in repairable claims; Belgian registrations breaking below the 400,000 plateau after the 1 January 2027 tax change.

Against the market. The sell-side knows the content story and the Automotive collapse, but it treats insurer pricing as an "investor debate" and models Belron's price and mix at 3 to 4 percent a year to 2029 (Bernstein). My base case is below that. I also think Belron's exposure to insurers runs as much through the mark-up over NAGS on complex glass (about 84 percent of revenue) as through calibration fees (8 percent of revenue), and nobody models the NAGS mark-up.

Conclusion. The external forces are strong and durable where D'Ieteren's profit sits and hostile where it does not, so the operating environment supports the case, while the market environment and a forming insurer headwind cap how fast the market can recognise it.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. The force that reaches the profit pool is structural and mandated: camera fitment from 49% to 60% of windscreens under EU GSR2, recalibration adding EUR 150-300 a job, a US claims-frequency recovery from 1.5% against a 2.1% average, the State Farm programme and a rising technical bar squeezing independents, plus PHE's ageing parc and TVH's recovery. Netted against it are the direct threats: US insurers starting to cap calibration and NAGS mark-ups, a mild El Nino winter, a weak US consumer, and a collapsing Belgian car market at Automotive, which falls from 17% to about 7% of profit. I sit above the group score of 56 because that score was anchored on flat group revenue, which is Automotive's shrinkage, while the profit-weighted balance is about 60/40 positive. That puts it a clear but offset positive, just above Linea Directa (a pricing cycle exposed to reversal) and below Eckert & Ziegler.

2

Internally driven corporate change

Evidence. D'Ieteren has moved from a phase of building and levering to a phase of deleveraging and crystallising value, and the last twelve months hold an unusual density of change. In the building phase (2019 to 2024), D'Ieteren bought TVH and PHE with cash from Belron capital reductions, Belron transformed its margin, and the EUR 4.2bn 2024 recapitalisation levered Belron. The changes of the last twelve months are as follows.

  • Belron's capital structure has been made ready for a listing. Net debt was EUR 8,343m at 4.3x EBITDA in June 2026, down from about 5.4x in late 2024. Belron repriced its term loans in July 2025 and January 2026 and received a contractual 25 basis-point margin step-down in October 2025. As a result, Belron's derived finance and other costs at 100 percent fell from about EUR 262m a half (H2 2025) to EUR 208m (H1 2026), an 18 percent fall that the company confirms; the USD term loan fell from USD 4,655m to USD 4,036m. Operationally, Belron's Transformation Program added 160 basis points of margin in H1 2026 after 180 in FY2025, cash conversion was 89 percent and the Net Promoter Score reached a record 87.
  • The Belron review began on 9 September 2026. Belron's private-equity co-owners (Clayton, Dubilier & Rice with 20 percent; Hellman & Friedman, GIC and BlackRock with 18 percent together) are formally evaluating liquidity options, including an Amsterdam listing at a mooted value of EUR 30 to 40bn, with Rothschild appointed as adviser. D'Ieteren keeps its 50.3 percent. KBC Securities calls EUR 30bn conservative and models EUR 34bn.
  • D'Ieteren's chief executive changes in December 2026. Eric Machiels (most recently at OMERS infrastructure; earlier at Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and Terra Firma, and eight years running Infinis Energy) replaces Francis Deprez, who led for ten years, delivered a 22 percent annualised ten-year total shareholder return and earned a leadership grade of B+. The chairman frames the next phase as one of "proactive ownership" and "disciplined capital allocation". The CFO who runs the budgeting, Edouard Janssen (who bought EUR 800k of shares in November 2025), and Belron's chief executive, Carlos Brito (formerly of AB InBev), both stay.
  • D'Ieteren Automotive is restructuring. On 3 September 2026, management presented the Works Council with a transformation plan affecting 344 roles (10 to 15 percent of the workforce), with site closures and cuts to marketing and consulting. The plan followed a 58.7 percent fall in Automotive's operating result in H1 2026 and a EUR 47.2m goodwill impairment. The savings and their timing depend on consultation under the Renault Act; my arithmetic puts the gross saving at EUR 30 to 35m a year.
  • The portfolio is moving at the edges. PHE bought 51 percent of Spain's Polaris and Regueira (about EUR 340m of sales, consolidated from 29 May 2026) and 80 percent of Suministros Dama. TVH appointed a new chief executive, Giuliano Parody, from 1 September 2026 after missing its 2025 targets. Moleskine has co-CEOs and a cost reset.
  • The holding is returning capital and has cut its own debt. A EUR 100m "solidarity" buyback that began in December 2025 had bought 405,702 shares for EUR 69.7m by 21 October 2026, taking treasury shares to 2.7 percent. The FY2025 dividend was flat at EUR 2.00 (FactSet's EUR 1.40 is a payment-period figure). The holding prepaid its EUR 500m bridge loan in 2025 and cut corporate net debt from EUR 653m to EUR 287m in a year.
  • Ambition was raised only at Belron. Belron's margin target rose from 23 percent (met in FY2025) to above 25 percent by FY2028. The other FY2028 ambitions (TVH 16 percent, Automotive about 4 percent, Moleskine 15 percent) were reaffirmed, not raised. FY2026 group guidance was set below consensus in March 2026 and confirmed in September.

Inference and so-what. The internal change is broad, real and financially resourced, and it points in one direction: toward a simpler, more transparent, better-capitalised Belron and a holding that returns more cash. The changes reach the earnings model through three incremental channels (Belron's finance costs, the Automotive cost base and PHE's first Spanish year) and reach the multiple through one large channel (the Belron event). The chief-executive change fits the crystallisation phase: a private-equity and infrastructure capital allocator is the profile a board hires to run a listing process and to decide what to do with Belron's cash afterwards.

Counter-case. The largest change is a choice announced, not an action taken: nobody has stated a venue, timing, structure or use of proceeds for the Belron review, and a secondary sale gives D'Ieteren a price, not cash. The leadership bench below the top is thin: the Chief Investment Officer left at end-2025 and was not replaced, head-office staff turnover rose from 7 to 12 percent, and group employee engagement fell from 84.9 to 80.4 percent. A new chief executive with a private-equity instinct could prefer acquisitions (the stated mandate is tickets of EUR 100m to 1bn) to buybacks at a 45 percent discount, and could rebase the FY2028 targets and write down Moleskine (ING models EUR 140m) in March 2027. Guidance has not been raised, and the perimeter is widening, not shrinking.

What would change my view. Positive: a capital-allocation statement at the May 2027 annual general meeting, or at a capital-markets day, that pairs the Belron process with a larger buyback or a Belron dividend policy. Negative: a first strategy statement led by an acquisition pipeline; the Belron review closing without a transaction; or the private-equity holders demanding a Belron dividend recapitalisation (the 2024 recapitalisation took Belron's leverage from about 3x to 5.4x).

Against the market. The sell-side reads the Belron review as the catalyst and prices it into unanimous Buy ratings and a EUR 230 median target, but takes no position on buybacks against acquisitions. I weight the new chief executive's first two decisions (the FY2027 framing on 10 March 2027 and the capital-allocation statement in May) more heavily than the market does, because those two decisions determine whether the earnings story and the event story reinforce or undercut each other.

Conclusion. The internal change forces are strong, well-resourced and correctly aimed, but the force that could move the shares most is still a review rather than a decision, and the new chief executive's first choices in March and May 2027 will decide whether the changes compound.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. The company's own actions are broad, funded and partly in the numbers: Belron cut leverage from 5.4x to 4.3x and its finance costs by 18% a half; its Transformation Program added 160bp of margin in H1 2026; its target was lifted to above 25%; there is a 344-role Automotive reset worth EUR 30-35m gross, a Spanish PHE deal and a 1%-a-year buyback; and the Belron listing review is a large strategic move, although it acts on the multiple more than on earnings. Weighed against these: a new chief executive arriving mid-review with a thin bench below him and engagement falling; TVH's and Moleskine's misses; a consultation that has given no savings number; and a risk that capital goes to acquisitions rather than buybacks. I sit above the group's 54 because the deleveraging and margin programme are already working in reported figures, which lifts it above Richard's 'gently positive, mediocre' CVS 55 but below OEM's active, delivered acquisition engine.

3

Value chain, business model, financial profile and management

Key message

Belron is one of the best-structured businesses in European services, but D'Ieteren holds Belron through a levered, family-first, equity-accounted wrapper, and the wrapper, not the moat, explains the discount.

Evidence: Belron's industry structure is the most favourable one an industry offers for share gain. Belron is the global number one in vehicle-glass repair, replacement and recalibration, with 17 to 19 percent of a EUR 40bn market. Belron's share is more than double Boyd's (7 to 8 percent), and the next players are Driven Brands (5 percent) and Cary Group (1 percent), above a tail of independents with over 70 percent. Four features make the structure favourable: a dominant leader over a fragmented tail; a technical barrier that rises with every model year; demand that safety regulation mandates and insurers pay for (70 to 77 percent of Belron's revenue); and competitors who held price when volume fell (US glass units fell 5 to 6 percent in 2024, while Belron's price and mix rose 5.1 percent in FY2025).

Belron's competitive advantages show up in behaviour in four of the five categories.

  • Customer integration. Safelite Solutions administers 65 to 75 percent of US non-collision glass claims and, since July 2025, State Farm's programme. Travelers and Liberty Mutual call Safelite their preferred vendor for its "unmatched national scale".
  • Production. Belron runs a proprietary supply chain, about 3,000 service centres and fleets of mobile vans, and it rolled out mobile static recalibration in the US in 2025 and in the UK in 2026.
  • Scale. Belron is the largest or second-largest buyer of glass, at about 10 million units a year. Domestic US sourcing from Fuyao's Ohio plant shields Safelite from the 25 percent tariff on glass that hurts import-dependent rivals.
  • Regulation. Camera mandates turn a glass job into a technical service.

Belron's outputs are top-decile. Belron's operating margin is 23.0 percent, up from 5.4 percent in 2017, against Boyd's structurally lower margin and 4.3 percent at Auto Glass Now. Belron's organic growth is 7.3 percent against peers near 3 percent; its gross margin is 62.4 percent; and its capital spending is only about 1.5 percent of revenue.

The other three businesses are a niche leader, a dented leader and a narrowing franchise. PHE is number one in French independent parts distribution (62 percent of its sales) and top three in Western Europe, in a market where the top seven players hold only 25 percent. PHE's logistics density (delivery within two hours on 90 percent of stock-keeping units from over 400 automated sites) and its digital platforms (over 30 percent of business-to-business orders) earn it a 9.1 to 9.6 percent margin. TVH holds over 50 percent of European forklift aftermarket parts (over 1 million stock-keeping units, 95 percent shipped the same day), although its 2023 cyber-attack dented its position. D'Ieteren Automotive holds a 78-year exclusive contract to distribute Volkswagen Group cars in Belgium: a franchise, not a competitive advantage, and a narrowing one.

Evidence: the financial profile is strong at the assets and middling at the holding. Four features of the holding's financial profile weigh on how the market prices D'Ieteren.

  • Reported returns are low. The group's reported return on invested capital is 5.1 percent, depressed by acquisition goodwill, equity accounting and Moleskine, against 11 percent at LKQ and 15 percent at Genuine Parts.
  • The gap between adjusted and reported earnings is wide and not closing. Adjusted EPS (EUR 12.95) is 61 percent above reported EPS (EUR 8.04). Belron's recurring "adjusting items" run at about EUR 130m a year, including EUR 44m of system-integrator fees that have appeared every year since 2023, and purchase-price amortisation is about EUR 57m at group share.
  • Costs below the operating line are heavy since the recapitalisation. Costs between the group-share operating result and PBT GS absorbed 30 percent of the operating result in FY2025 (EUR 412m of EUR 1,367m).
  • Cash reaches the holding late. Free cash flow to the holding is only about 40 percent of adjusted net income in FY2026 and FY2027 (EUR 292m and EUR 316m), rising toward 57 percent by FY2030 (EUR 597m) as Belron's dividends to D'Ieteren grow from about EUR 103m to EUR 260m. Belron already pays about EUR 400m a year of dividends at 100 percent, and paid EUR 1.8bn in 2021 and EUR 4.2bn in the 2024 recapitalisation. Fitch's trigger for upgrading Belron requires a free-cash-flow margin after dividends above 2 percent, so Belron's dividend path and its ratings path pull against each other.

Evidence: management's big strategic moves were right and bold. Management rotated a Belgian car importer into aftermarket compounders, backed calibration early, and funded the TVH and PHE purchases from Belron capital reductions (paying 9.3x EV/EBIT for PHE).

The group's delivery record is strong, and the misses sit outside Belron. The group beat its guidance in each of the four years from FY2022 to FY2025. TVH missed its 2025 targets by more than 12 percent on sales and by 30 percent on free cash flow; Moleskine's profit fell 34 and 50 percent; Automotive missed H1 2026 consensus by 51 percent, and management was "less transparent" about Automotive's share loss.

Culture is congruent inside Belron and not across the group. Employee engagement is 87 percent at Belron, 77 percent at TVH and 72 percent at Moleskine.

Governance puts the family first. Five million participating shares give Nayarit, the family holding, 53.84 percent of the votes on 49.54 percent of the capital. The 2024 reorganisation financed one family branch's buy-out of another through a EUR 74 per share special dividend, funded by Belron debt that took Belron's credit rating to junk. Executives have no shareholding requirements; half of any buyback outperformance goes to family foundations; seven of the twelve directors are independent. A 27-person head office runs six businesses and claims no synergies between them.

Inference and so-what. D'Ieteren's moat is strong but sits almost entirely in one asset, so the group's earnings quality and multiple depend on one variable (Belron's realised price and how much of it drops through to profit) far more than the six-business perimeter suggests. The financial profile explains the discount better than the moat does: low reported returns, a wide gap between adjusted and reported earnings, a levered subsidiary, cash that reaches the holding late, and a governance ordering the market has not forgiven since 2024. For the model, management's credibility justifies taking Belron's targets at face value and leaning slightly above FY2026 guidance; it does not justify taking the Automotive, TVH and Moleskine targets at face value, and the base case does not.

Counter-case. Belron kept almost all of its scale economies as margin (5.4 to 23 percent) and shared them with insurers only indirectly, through service quality. Concentrated buyers who watch a supplier's margin quadruple claw part of it back, and US insurers are now beginning to do so. Automotive's sole supplier, Volkswagen, is restructuring and may seek savings on the distributor's margin or move to an agency model; the precedent is BYD taking its Benelux distribution in-house from Inchcape when Inchcape's contract expires in Q3 2027. Finally, the holding's reported return on invested capital of 5 percent is what most stock screens see.

What would change my view. Belron losing a major claims-administration mandate, or an insurer publicly separating claims administration from repair (GEICO already uses LYNX to avoid Safelite's dual role); evidence, with launch dates, that carmakers can self-calibrate windscreen cameras (today the engineering view is that a replaced windscreen needs a manual baseline recalibration, and the threat lies after 2030); Volkswagen moving to agency terms in Belgium.

Against the market. The sell-side values Belron at 17 to 27x EBIT on comparables (Boyd and Driven at about 17x; best-in-class services at 27x; Cary Group bought at 26x EBITA and mooted for sale above EUR 3bn), and I agree that Belron deserves that company. I differ on the holding: the governance component of D'Ieteren's discount (37 to 45 percent, against 28 to 32 percent at GBL and Sofina) does not disappear with a listing, so I would not capitalise Belron's moat at the parent as if the wrapper did not exist.

Conclusion. Belron's value chain and business model are among the best-structured in European services and compound mechanically, but D'Ieteren holds Belron through a levered, family-first, equity-accounted wrapper whose financial profile and governance justify a discount that Belron's quality alone cannot close.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Belron is a near-best-in-class chain: a dominant leader with 17-19% share over a 70% independent tail, a barrier that rises with every model year, mandated and insurer-paid demand, behaviourally evidenced moats, a margin rising from 5.4% to 23% and about 1.5% capital intensity; PHE and TVH are niche leaders. The figures mislead both ways: the 92nd-percentile ROIC and 18th-percentile operating margin are the consolidated Automotive-heavy perimeter, the holding's true reported ROIC is 5.1%, there is a 61% adjusted-to-reported gap, and the cash reaching the parent is levered and late. With family-first governance and misses outside Belron, the parts are coherent with the groups (72, 76, 50, 60). That places it just below Tele2's clean oligopoly and above Carlsberg.

4

Guidance conservatism, expectation management and the delivery record

Evidence: D'Ieteren sets low bars and clears them. In March 2026 the company guided FY2026 PBT GS up by a low-to-mid-single-digit percentage at constant currency (at EUR/USD 1.17), 7 to 9 percent below consensus. On 9 September it confirmed that guidance despite a 66.6 percent fall in Automotive's PBT, and H1 2026 PBT GS came in up 8.4 percent at constant currency. The base case of EUR 992m (+3.8 percent reported, about +5.5 percent at constant currency) sits at the top of the implied EUR 975 to 1,005m range, and Deutsche Bank (EUR 984m) and Jefferies (EUR 1,014m) bracket it.

The delivery record is long. The group beat guidance in each year from FY2022 to FY2025. FY2025 PBT GS of EUR 955.6m beat the company-compiled consensus of EUR 926.6m by 3.1 percent, in a year of a strong euro, high rates and US claims avoidance. H1 2026 group PBT GS landed within 0.3 percent of consensus even though Automotive came in 51 percent below, because Belron beat by 5 percent, TVH by 20 percent and PHE by 5 percent.

The company does raise guidance mid-year, contrary to an earlier reading, but only when Belron is far ahead and the other units are clean. In September 2022 it raised growth guidance from at least 25 percent to 35 percent and delivered 50.9 percent; in September 2023 it raised from about EUR 900m to above EUR 960m and delivered EUR 970.8m. In 2024, 2025 and 2026, when one unit was failing, it confirmed rather than raised.

The sell-side's cutting cycle has ended but not reversed. Over twelve months, FactSet mean EPS fell 12.3 percent for FY2026, 10.9 percent for FY2027 and 4.5 percent for FY2028; over the last month, the changes were only minus 0.6, minus 0.2 and plus 0.1 percent. All ten visible brokers rate the shares Buy or Overweight, with a median target of EUR 230.

The brokers disagree mostly on accounting basis, not on substance. Two brokers at EUR 9.81 and EUR 10.00 for FY2026 EPS appear to be on a reported or equity-accounted basis, so the median of EUR 13.40, not the mean of EUR 12.75, is the right anchor. The genuine disagreements concern Automotive (Bernstein at a 1.7 percent FY2028 margin against Deutsche Bank near 4 percent) and TVH; brokers' Belron estimates cluster within about 1 percent of consensus.

Inference and so-what. D'Ieteren's guidance is conservative by habit and will stay conservative under a new chief executive who inherits the habit and arrives during an unresolved Belgian consultation. The guidance events of the next eighteen months are therefore a source of beats, not of raised bars, with one scheduled exception.

The exception is 10 March 2027, when the FY2027 framing is more likely to land below consensus than in line. The likely wording is "mid-to-high-single-digit" or "high-single-digit" growth at constant currency, against a consensus of about +14 percent in PBT GS and +16 percent in EPS. The precedent for the share-price reaction is March 2026, when a below-consensus framing took consensus FY2026 EPS down about 5 percent over the following quarter and took the shares down with it. The mitigants this time are an FY2026 beat and a Belron margin near 24 percent printed on the same day, and brokers who already model the divergence between segments, so I expect consensus cuts of 2 to 4 percent, not 5.

September 2027 is the test of whether guidance is raised. A raise needs Belron's H1 2027 organic growth at 6 percent or more with its margin at or above 24.5 percent, Automotive stabilised with a social plan agreed, and EUR/USD at or below 1.20.

70% / 22% / 8%
10 March 2027 FY2027 framing: below / in line with / above consensus
45% / 45% / 10%
September 2027: guidance raised / confirmed / cut

Counter-case. New chief executives rebase. The March 2027 statement could also retire the Automotive (4 percent) and Moleskine (15 percent) margin targets and write Moleskine down, and a "kitchen sink" of charges that coincides with a cautious framing would deepen the air pocket. I put the odds of a kitchen sink at about 30 percent, because the balance-sheet clean-ups at Automotive and Moleskine are largely done. Separately, because guidance is framed at constant currency, a reported miss can coexist with guidance met if the dollar weakens.

What would change my view. An FY2027 framing of "double-digit" growth in March, which would signal that the new chief executive has broken the habit and would remove the air pocket; or an FY2026 outcome below the middle of the range, which would say that the H2 2026 softness at Automotive and TVH was worse than the run-rate implies.

Against the market. Consensus has the level of FY2027 earnings right and the presentation risk wrong: the market treats the company as a pure sandbagger and has forgotten that it raised guidance in 2022 and 2023. I expect the sequence beat (March), dip (the framing), recovery (second quarter) and raise test (September), and the market is not positioned for that sequence.

Conclusion. Current guidance is conservative, the delivery record is strong at the group and clean at Belron, and the next eighteen months hold more beats than misses, with one scheduled presentation disappointment on 10 March 2027 that is the expected course of events rather than evidence against the case.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. The group has beaten guidance in FY2022-FY2025 and raised mid-year in 2022 and 2023, and FY2026 guidance was set 7-9% below consensus, with H1 at +8.4% at constant currency against a low-to-mid-single-digit guide, so the current guide is conservative. Against that, consensus EPS was cut 11-12% over twelve months on Automotive and TVH, TVH missed its 2025 targets, Automotive missed H1 consensus by 51%, and the March 2027 framing will likely sit below consensus. That is a reliable group institution with a dented record on raising sell-side estimates, between the guidance group (64) and the memo's reading, below Odfjell's cleaner beats and just above Avanza.

5

Operating leverage, financial leverage, pricing power, cost-out and feedback loops: why revenue growth becomes outsized profit growth

Evidence: five mechanisms turn slow revenue growth into fast EPS growth. Group-share revenue grows only about 3.4 percent a year from FY2025 to FY2030, because Automotive's revenue shrinks from 41 percent to 32 percent of the total and grows about zero. Yet PBT GS grows about 9.8 percent a year to FY2028 and EPS about 10.9 percent.

  • Belron's operating leverage is high, and the base case fades it. Calibration carries an 80 to 90 percent incremental gross margin once the equipment and technicians are in place. Workshop density economics are steep: a two-technician site loses money below two replacements a day and reaches a 40 percent margin at eight. Belron's incremental margin in H1 2026 was 59 percent reported (about 47 percent at constant currency). The base case fades the incremental margin from 43 percent (FY2026) to 36 percent (FY2028) and 30 percent (FY2030), for two reasons: insurers are moving to regulate the highest-margin content (calibration fees and NAGS mark-ups on complex glass), and inflation in labour and mobile equipment absorbs part of the gain. The leverage works in both directions: in 2012 a mild winter cut organic sales by 4.4 percent and the operating result by 24 percent, while in 2020 management flexed labour and held the EBITDA margin above 10 percent through a 17 percent fall in volume.
  • Fixed costs below the operating line gear profit growth. With about EUR 330 to 345m of finance and other costs under a group-share operating result of EUR 1.3 to 1.6bn, every 1 percent of operating growth becomes about 1.3 to 1.4 percent of PBT growth. Of the 9.8 percent a year PBT growth to FY2028, this pure gearing supplies about 2.1 points and finance-cost relief about 2.4 points.
  • Belron's finance-cost relief is front-loaded in FY2026. Belron's finance and other costs at 100 percent fall from EUR 516m in FY2025 to EUR 416m in FY2026. That EUR 100m step (from repricings, the margin step-down, a weaker dollar on USD debt and the first year of deleveraging) is worth about EUR 50m of PBT GS and is already in the H1 2026 run-rate. After FY2026, deleveraging of EUR 550 to 650m a year saves only about EUR 30m a year at 100 percent (EUR 15m at group share, about 1.3 percent of EPS a year). The 2029 notes (EUR 850m at 4.625 percent and USD 1,115m at 5.75 percent) will refinance at today's high-yield services rate of about 7.5 percent, adding about EUR 41m a year at 100 percent from Q4 2029.
  • Pricing power is real at Belron, a pass-through at PHE and TVH, and negative at Automotive. Belron passes 10 to 20 percent glass inflation through semi-annual clauses indexed to NAGS (the September 2025 NAGS update lifted list prices 5.6 percent, a tailwind that annualises in H2 2026), holds a 25 percent price premium with US cash-paying customers, and kept price when volume fell. Calibration is only about 8 percent of Belron's revenue (Bernstein), so each five points of calibration penetration adds under one point of revenue; most of Belron's 3.4 to 5.1 percent price and mix comes from complex glass priced off NAGS. PHE's parts prices rose 1.5 percent quarter on quarter in Q2 2026, a margin-neutral pass-through; TVH's pricing is "highly constrained"; and Automotive's price and mix is negative (Volkswagen's EUR 6,000 discounts on its ID electric models, competition from Chinese plug-in hybrids).
  • About EUR 45 to 55m of identifiable cost savings reach PBT GS by FY2028, about 4 percent of it, and almost none arrive before H2 2027. The savings are: Automotive EUR 15m net in FY2027 and EUR 30m by FY2028, after Belgian consultation and wage indexation; TVH's ramp-up costs at Poland and Reno falling away (about EUR 8m at group share); PHE's Spanish procurement synergies (EUR 8 to 10m by FY2029); and Moleskine's cost reset. Belron's efficiency gains are embedded in its margin path and are not a cost-cutting story.
  • The buyback retires about 1 percent of shares a year. The buyback runs at about EUR 80 to 100m a year, and SPDG's five-year sell-down of its family stake supplies the float.

Three reinforcing feedback loops drive Belron for the next eighteen months, and one balancing loop dominates after that. The reinforcing loops are content routing volume to the scaled operator (R1), the State Farm administration role deepening density and purchasing scale (R2, a one-time step that I do not extrapolate beyond FY2027), and cash generation lowering leverage and interest (R3). The balancing loop is insurers responding to Belron's retained margin with caps, documentation rules and hourly pricing (B4). Loop B4 is the main reason the base case sits about 1.5 percent below consensus for FY2028 and about 10 percent below the two-broker FY2029 figure.

Outside Belron, one loop is being interrupted and one is weak until FY2029. At Automotive, a downward reinforcing loop (lower volume, fixed-cost deleverage at a 24 percent decremental margin, share loss, impairment) is being interrupted by the restructuring, which floors the margin without reversing the volume decline. At the holding, the cash loop stays weak until FY2029, when Belron's leverage approaches 3x and its dividends to D'Ieteren rise; only then does the holding have EUR 140 to 280m a year of surplus to fund larger buybacks or acquisitions.

Inference and so-what. The conversion of revenue into profit is strong, evidenced and front-loaded. FY2026 is a finance-cost year; FY2027 and FY2028 are operations years, with Belron's margin rising about 80 basis points a year; and from FY2029 EPS growth slows to 7 to 8 percent as both engines fade. The composition matters for the multiple: a market that discounts finance-driven growth (as Viewforth's research library documents for the transmission of leverage into EPS) should pay more for the FY2027 to FY2028 growth than for FY2026's growth, and the sell-side has not yet made that distinction.

Counter-case. The cost structure that delivers incremental margins of about 45 percent on the way up delivers decremental margins of 40 to 50 percent on the way down: a relapse in volume (from the consumer or the weather) costs about EUR 50m of PBT GS for every 3 points of lost organic growth over a year. Floating-rate debt is 77 percent of Belron's debt, with an undisclosed hedge ratio, so loop R3 turns into a drag if SOFR rises. A dividend recapitalisation of Belron after a listing would reverse the finance relief.

What would change my view. Belron printing an incremental margin below 30 percent in H2 2026 or H1 2027 without a volume explanation, which would say the insurer pricing loop is biting earlier than modelled; or Belron's leverage stalling above 4x, which would say dividends or acquisitions are absorbing the cash.

Against the market. The sell-side calls interest relief "a primary driver" of 2027 to 2028 growth; on my build, finance relief supplies 11 percent of it. The market also treats Belron's price and mix as a calibration story, whereas it is mostly a story of complex glass priced off NAGS, which changes what investors should monitor.

Conclusion. Revenue growth of 3 to 4 percent becomes EPS growth of 10 to 11 percent through Belron's operating leverage, gearing below the operating line, front-loaded finance relief, cost-out from mid-2027 and a 1 percent buyback; the conversion is strongest in FY2027 to FY2028 and fades afterwards as the insurers' balancing loop engages.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. Several gears are proven at Belron. Calibration carries 80-90% incremental gross margin. Workshop density economics are steep, with incremental margin of 43-59%, and they cut both ways (2012: sales -4.4%, operating result -24%). Pricing power is real: NAGS-indexed pass-through, a 25% cash-pay premium, and price held while volume fell. Below the operating line, gearing and finance relief turn 1% of operating growth into 1.3-1.4% of PBT, there is EUR 45-55m of cost-out from mid-2027, and three reinforcing loops are at work. Together they turn about 3.4% revenue growth into about 11% EPS growth, about 3x against the Universe's 2x. It falls short of 90 because the financial leverage is junk-rated and 77% floating rather than comfortable, the insurer balancing loop is already fading incremental margins to 30%, and Automotive's 24% decremental gearing runs in reverse, so it sits above the economic-strength group's 50, which weighed the holding's drag rather than the structure.

The base case delivers two years of 13 to 15 percent EPS growth (FY2027 and FY2028) and a record group-share margin, and no single earnings judgement moves FY2028 EPS by more than about 5 percent; one turn of P/E moves the share price by about 12 percent.

The half-years show growth stalling in H2 2026 and then reaccelerating to about 13 percent in 2027. H2 2026 PBT GS should be about EUR 509m (+1.2 percent): Belron adds about EUR 52m on lower finance costs and an operating result near EUR 865m at 100 percent, PHE adds EUR 10m, and Automotive falls by about EUR 66m from H2 2025's EUR 106m. H1 2027 PBT GS should be about EUR 547m (+13.4 percent), and H2 2027 about EUR 580m (+13.8 percent), as restructuring savings begin and Automotive's comparison becomes easy.

D'Ieteren has scope for double-digit growth and for higher margins than in the past, but only for two years and with a precise shape. EPS grows 14.5 percent in FY2027 and 13.3 percent in FY2028, then 9.3 percent and 7.5 percent. The group-share margin rises from 11.3 percent to 12.3 percent by FY2028, about half the pace of FY2023 to FY2025 (about 55 basis points a year), for two reasons. First, Belron's margin gains halve, from 150 to 180 basis points a year recently (and 319 in H2 2025) to about 80 a year. Second, Automotive's margin sits on a 2 to 3 percent plateau rather than the 4.7 to 5.1 percent that the post-pandemic order backlog and battery-electric mix flattered.

The forward period is more legible than the history. Unlike any of the last six years, the forecast period has a stable perimeter: no TVH or PHE deal, no backlog boom and no recapitalisation.

The base case meets the company's FY2028 ambitions for Belron and deliberately falls short of them elsewhere. For Belron, the base case has a 25.3 percent margin against "above 25 percent" and 5.5 percent organic growth against "above 5 percent". It sets TVH's margin at 14.5 percent against a 16 percent target, Automotive's at 3.0 percent against about 4 percent, and Moleskine's at about 7 percent against 15 percent. Those three units account for most of the gap between the base case and the company's implied FY2028 ambition, and they are where the sell-side's estimates disperse.

The risks to the base case lean neutral for FY2027 and slightly down for FY2028. Belron's operating line and the finance line lean up: Belron's H2 2025 margin of 24.4 percent makes FY2026's 23.9 percent conservative by 20 to 30 basis points, and Bernstein's FY2028 path reaches 26.0 percent against the base case's 25.3 percent, a EUR 28m difference at group share. Automotive, TVH and Moleskine lean down. I keep every model input unchanged.

The five judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic. EPS effects use PBT GS x 0.72 / 51.55m shares (FY2028) unless stated; 1 percent of FY2028 EPS is about EUR 0.18.

1
Belron's realised price and how much of it drops through to profit (the insurer loop). Base case: price and mix of 3.0 percent (FY2027) and 2.5 percent (FY2028), with drop-through falling from 70 to about 55 percent, giving margins of 24.7 and 25.3 percent. If the FY2028 margin is 100 basis points lower: 1 percent x Belron revenue of EUR 7,860m = EUR 79m of operating result at 100 percent; x 50.3 percent = EUR 40m of PBT GS; x 0.72 / 51.55m = EUR 0.55 of EPS, or 3.1 percent. If Bernstein's 26.0 percent is right: +70 basis points = +EUR 28m = +EUR 0.39 of EPS. If US insurers cut calibration prices by 20 percent in a coordinated move: calibration revenue of about EUR 540m, about 60 percent of it in the US, x 20 percent = EUR 65m at close to full drop-through; x 50.3 percent = EUR 33m, or EUR 0.45 of EPS (2.6 percent); the base case already carries about a third of that cut by FY2028. Monitor: NAGS updates; policy statements from State Farm, Travelers and Liberty Mutual; Belron's reported price and mix.
2
Belron's volume (the US consumer, the winter and market share). Base case: volume +3.5 percent (FY2026) and +3.0 percent (FY2027 and FY2028). If volume runs 3 points below plan for a year: 3 percent x EUR 7,450m = EUR 224m of revenue; at a 45 percent decremental margin = EUR 100m at 100 percent, EUR 50m of PBT GS and EUR 0.70 of EPS (4.5 percent of FY2027's EUR 15.60). A mild winter half costs about half of that (EUR 24m, EUR 0.33 of EPS). The 2020 precedent says management can flex labour when the shock is visible, which halves the decremental margin. Monitor: Boyd's repairable claims; same-store sales at Driven's Auto Glass Now; US winter weather; premium inflation.
3
The floor under Automotive's margin. Base case: margin of 2.6 percent (FY2027) and 3.0 percent (FY2028) on revenue of EUR 4,330m and EUR 4,395m, with net savings of EUR 15m in FY2027 and EUR 30m by FY2028. Each 50 basis points of margin is EUR 22m of PBT GS, or EUR 0.30 of EPS (1.7 percent). Bernstein's 1.7 percent FY2028 margin against the base case's 3.0 percent is 130 basis points x EUR 4,395m = EUR 57m, or EUR 0.80 of EPS (4.5 percent): the bear tail. A social plan slipping to late 2027 costs about EUR 8m (EUR 0.11 of EPS); a 10 percent drop in fleet sales after the 1 January 2027 tax change costs a further EUR 10 to 15m. Monitor: Febiac's monthly Belgian registrations; Belgian union reports; Volkswagen's distribution terms.
4
Belron's cost of debt. Base case: finance and other costs of EUR 385m (FY2027) and EUR 355m (FY2028) at 100 percent. A 100 basis-point rise in floating rates costs EUR 30m at 100 percent if about half of the EUR 6.0bn of term loans is unhedged (EUR 15m of PBT GS, EUR 0.21 of EPS, 1.2 percent), and up to EUR 60m if none is hedged (EUR 0.42, 2.4 percent). Refinancing the 2029 notes at 7.5 percent adds EUR 41m at 100 percent, EUR 21m of PBT GS and EUR 0.30 of EPS from Q4 2029 (the FY2030 base case allows for about half). Beyond the horizon, or sooner if a listing includes a primary raise, repaying one turn of leverage (about EUR 2.1bn at 6 percent) saves EUR 125m at 100 percent, EUR 63m of PBT GS and EUR 0.87 of EPS. A 5 percent move in EUR/USD moves EPS by EUR 0.27 (2 percent); one point on the tax rate moves EPS by 1.4 percent.
5
The multiple and the holding discount (the Belron event). This judgement moves the shares without moving EPS. On two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 19.9 at end-2027 (implied by the model's EUR 205 value at 10.29x), each turn of P/E is worth about EUR 20 a share, about 12 percent of today's price. Moving from the guideline 10.29x to the ten-year median of 11.0x adds EUR 14 (+8 percent); to the 75th percentile of 12.1x adds EUR 36 (+21 percent); and falling to the 10th percentile of 9.3x costs EUR 20 (minus 12 percent). In terms of the discount to Jefferies' net asset value of EUR 317 a share, today's 45 percent discount implies EUR 174; a 35 percent discount gives EUR 206 (+21 percent); and the ten-year average discount of 30 percent gives EUR 222 (+30 percent). A listing at the EUR 30bn bottom of the mooted range values D'Ieteren's 50.3 percent of Belron's equity (EUR 30bn less EUR 8.3bn of net debt, x 50.3 percent) at about EUR 10.9bn, above the group's whole market capitalisation of about EUR 9.0bn on 52.25m ordinary shares. At Jefferies' EUR 33.8bn, the stake is worth about EUR 245 a share.

The combined stress case cuts FY2028 EPS by about 9 to 10 percent, to about EUR 16.0. The stress case combines a Belron margin 100 basis points lower (the full calibration cut), Automotive at 2.5 percent, rates up 100 basis points on the unhedged half of the term loans, EUR/USD at 1.25 and a 29 percent tax rate. These stresses are correlated, because a weak US consumer, insurer cost pressure and higher US rates arrive together, so they belong in one case, with a joint probability of perhaps 15 percent. The bull case raises FY2028 EPS by about 5 percent, to about EUR 18.6, on Belron at a 26 percent margin, Automotive at 3.5 percent, a Belron ratings upgrade and early PHE synergies.

Against the market. The base case is within 2 percent of consensus for FY2026 to FY2028 (slightly above in FY2026, slightly below in FY2028) and about 10 percent below the two-broker FY2029 figure, which extrapolates FY2027 to FY2028 growth that the fading of both Belron engines does not support.

Conclusion. The base case offers two years of 13 to 15 percent EPS growth and a group-share margin rising to a record 12.3 percent by FY2028, built almost entirely on Belron's demonstrated engine and a floor under Automotive. The EPS range is tight for FY2026, moderate for FY2027 and skewed down for FY2028 by one named, monitorable variable: Belron's realised price.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. 10-15% gives B, and the measure sits near the floor of the band. I place it slightly above the floor because the growth is organic on a stable perimeter (PHE Spain is small) and the group-share margin rises to a record 12.3% by FY2028. It stays low in the band because the growth is front-loaded: 14.5% and 13.3% in FY2027-28, fading to 7-8%, with FY2026 driven by finance costs, and the margin gains run at half the recent pace.

7

Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over the coming six to twelve months

Evidence and inference: the revision cycle has ended, not reversed. The twelve-month cuts of 11 to 12 percent to FY2026 and FY2027 EPS came from Automotive and TVH, and those cuts are now in the numbers. One-month revisions are flat, and brokers' stand-alone estimates for Belron have been drifting up (Bernstein raised its Belron estimates after H1 2026).

The breadth of revisions should turn neutral by the FY2026 results and positive from September 2027 (about 55 percent likely). The Viewforth Master Dashboard's revision-momentum score should therefore move from minus 5 toward zero by spring 2027 and turn positive in the autumn.

Guidance is more likely to move up than down over eighteen months, after a cautious start in March. FY2026 guidance should be met at or above the top of its range (about 85 percent likely to be met or beaten). FY2027 guidance is likely to be framed below consensus in March (70 percent) and is more likely to be raised than cut in September (45 against 10 percent). Belron's FY2028 ambition is more likely to be raised than cut (about 40 percent likely to be raised, at a capital-markets day or in a listing prospectus, because a listing's equity story demands it). A new 2030 framework from the new chief executive within eighteen months is about 55 percent likely; it would most plausibly raise Belron's targets, retire Automotive's and Moleskine's margin targets and add the capital-allocation statement the market lacks.

The sell-side already tells the bull case and leaves out both the positive refinement and the negatives. The sell-side narrative covers Belron's compounding, its deleveraging, the listing and the discount, and prices them in unanimous Buy ratings and 34 percent upside to the median target. The narrative omits the operating composition of FY2027 to FY2028 growth (the positive refinement), the re-basing of insurer pricing and the missing Automotive savings figure (the negatives), and the precedent that a listing works only when paired with buybacks. No retail or forum narrative exists for a Belgian mid-cap with EUR 20 to 25m of daily turnover. The only investor voices are AVI Global Trust, which points to a discount near 50 percent and sees the listing as the unlock, and Berenberg, which warns that direct access to a listed Belron could widen D'Ieteren's discount unless D'Ieteren meets the listing with buybacks.

So-what. The scope for upgrades over the next six to twelve months is modest in level, because the base case sits at consensus, but favourable in timing and quality. The next twelve months contain the two events that turn revision breadth positive (the FY2026 beat and the H1 2027 delivery), and the narrative shift that matters, from "interest relief" to "operating growth", is the kind of shift that moves the multiple more than the estimates. The one dated air pocket, the March 2027 framing, sits between the two positive events.

Counter-case. A narrative that already contains the bull case and omits the bear case tilts the balance of surprise against the shares. The first public insurer move on pricing, or a delay to the Belgian social plan, would be new to the sell-side's models even though industry experts already know about both risks.

What would change my view. Belron reaching a 25 percent margin in FY2027 with volume growth holding above 3 percent, which would bring FY2027 to FY2028 upgrades of 2 to 4 percent and strongly positive breadth; or a relapse in the US consumer combined with a mild winter, which would bring FY2027 cuts of 3 to 5 percent between March and May 2027.

Against the market. The market expects the listing to be the upgrade; I expect the operating composition of growth to be the upgrade, and the listing to set the price.

Conclusion. The scope for upgrades is small in level but well-timed and good in quality: a dip in March 2027, then a turn in the second quarter and a raise test in September, and the market's recognition that the growth is operational is worth more than the estimate changes themselves.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Over the next 6-12 months, guidance is likely to beat on FY2026 (+1-2% to consensus) but then be framed below FY2027 consensus in March (about 70%, a 2-4% cut), with a September raise at 45% against a 10% cut. FY2028 is likely to drift down 1-3%. Net, the line that drives the price is likely to change about nil against about 3% revenue growth, roughly the 40th-percentile ratio. The narrative's shift from interest relief to operating growth, and the listing, add a modest positive, coherent with the fourth-set group's 57 but trimmed for the scheduled March dip. That puts it just below Theon's flat revisions with a backlog cushion and just above RELX's small, steady beats.

Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and the same for key peers

Key message

Momentum is weak on every measure but valuation, and the slope has stopped falling: the stock is cheap, moving badly and trading on its own news.

Evidence: the Viewforth Master Dashboard's pinned ratings at 29 October 2026 are weak on everything except valuation. Technical momentum is D, sell-side earnings momentum F, valuation B, thematic fit F, and the total-shareholder-return-to-valuation rating D.

The share price sits just below a flattening 200-day average. The price of EUR 171.3 is 1.3 percent below the 200-day average of EUR 173.5, which has risen in only six of the last twelve months. The 52-week range is EUR 141.8 to 197.4, and the stock's relative strength sits at the 31st percentile of the universe.

Sell-side revisions are still negative on every horizon for FY2027, while the share price is down over three to nine months and up over twelve.
