The target price has moved minus 2, 0 and plus 1 percent over the dashboard's periods. The share of Buy ratings is 79 percent (down 6 points in a month, up 9 points over six months), and the revision-momentum score is minus 5. Guidance momentum is flat (confirmed, not raised). Narrative momentum has been positive on the Belron event since 9 September and negative on Automotive.

The sector has split: the market rewards parts, services and rental, and punishes car retail and leasing. Inter Cars, a parts distributor, has returned +92.4 percent over twelve months with A-rated earnings momentum, while Inchcape and Auto1, both car retailers, have fallen 16.5 and 39.6 percent. D'Ieteren's own price moves owe little to the sector: over the latest six months the sector basket explains only 19 percent of its daily variance. That share rises toward 45 to 50 percent around the sector's results seasons (June to August) and falls to single digits when company news dominates, as it has since 9 September.

Liquidity is thin, and a family shareholder is a standing seller. Average daily volume is about 54,700 shares (about USD 20 to 25m); the free float is 39 percent; SPDG, a family shareholder, is selling about 9 to 10 percent of the company over five years; and short interest is below the disclosure threshold.

Inference and so-what. Momentum is weak on every pinned measure, but its slope has changed. The twelve-month revisions describe a cutting cycle that the one-month figures say has ended, and the technical D reflects a stock that has round-tripped on its own news, from EUR 190 (January 2026) to EUR 156 (March) to EUR 179 (July) to EUR 163 (September).

The peer evidence is both a warning and an invitation. The market pays for aftermarket businesses that are independent of any one carmaker (Inter Cars) and punishes retailers tied to one carmaker (Inchcape). D'Ieteren is four-fifths aftermarket by profit, yet the market rates it like neither group, because the stock trades on itself. That idiosyncrasy cuts both ways: a sector recovery would lift D'Ieteren only 0.6 for 1, and a sector sell-off would hurt it less. The 10 March 2027 result and the Belron process, not the sector, will set the multiple.

Counter-case. Technical momentum of D and a falling 200-day average are not the entry conditions the Viewforth framework rewards. The next sector results window (February to March 2027) coincides with D'Ieteren's own results; if the sector is weak then, the stock's beta rises toward 0.9 to 1.0 and the market reads D'Ieteren's result through the sector's lens for some weeks. The share of Buy ratings, already near 80 percent, has little room to rise and room to fall.

What would change my view. The price regaining its 200-day average while the revision score crosses zero, which would signal that the second-quarter 2027 turn is under way; or a break below EUR 156 (the March 2026 low and the previous memo's trigger for re-opening the case), which would say the market is pricing the failure of the Belron event.

Against the market. The dashboard's F for sell-side momentum looks twelve months into the rear-view mirror; I read the current slope as flat and turning. The market's framing that the shares "trade with car retail" is not supported by the data: the shares trade with nothing but themselves.

Conclusion. Momentum is weak and bottoming rather than turning: the revision cycle has ended, the technicals have not yet confirmed a turn, the peers that look like Belron are rewarded and the peers that look like Automotive are punished, and the stock will take its cue from its own March 2027 events rather than from either peer group.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Both measures are below 50, which gives D. The parts confirm D rather than F or C: guidance was confirmed, not raised; three-month FY2027 EPS revisions of -4% are more than 1x the roughly 3% revenue growth; the price sits 1.3% below a 200-day average rising in only half the last twelve months; and the narrative is positive on the Belron event, negative on Automotive. I place it mid-band because one-month revisions are flat (the cutting cycle has ended), the Buy share is at the 81st percentile and the price sits only just below its averages; comparable aftermarket peers are rewarded, but they do not lift the letter.

9

Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key message

Over eighteen months the earnings are more predictable than the wrapper looks; beyond eighteen months they are less predictable than Belron's record implies, and the share-price risks are perception risks that land without a sector cushion.

Simplicity of the case: simple to state, concentrated to hold. Two operating drivers carry about 70 percent of the FY2026 to FY2028 rise in PBT GS: Belron's price and mix with its drop-through, and the floor under Automotive's margin. One asset, Belron, carries 65 percent of profit and 77 percent of value. Belron's insurer customers pay 70 to 77 percent of its revenue and account for 40 percent of its North American jobs and 80 percent of its eurozone jobs. The offset to the concentration is that the concentrated driver has the best disclosure, the longest record and the tightest broker agreement, while the diffuse remainder (Automotive, TVH, Moleskine and corporate costs) is small and is where the earlier analysis rounds' errors and the sell-side's disputes sit.

The case requires five assumptions to hold.

  1. US insurers re-base calibration and NAGS pricing gradually, through rolling renewals, rather than in a coordinated move. The evidence (carrier-by-carrier flat rates and studies) supports a gradual re-basing.
  2. The US volume recovery survives a weak consumer and an El Nino winter.
  3. Automotive's consultation under the Renault Act yields a social plan by mid-2027. Belgian precedents ran from six months (Audi Brussels) to two years (Caterpillar Gosselies), and Audi's closure cost Volkswagen EUR 1.2bn of charges.
  4. No Belron recapitalisation follows a listing.
  5. The holding's cash stays adequate. The holding must fund the PHE put option at end-2026 (EUR 194m, more likely EUR 200 to 215m), within EUR 307m of further subsidiary put options, plus Spain's working capital and EUR 40 to 60m of Automotive restructuring cash in FY2027. Against those needs it has EUR 123m of corporate cash, an undrawn EUR 425m facility and EUR 218m of subsidiary dividends received in H1 2026. The needs are funded, but they are why consolidated net debt does not fall until FY2028.

The range of EPS outcomes widens with the horizon and is skewed down. FY2026 EPS should land between EUR 13.45 and 13.85, because H1 is reported and the H2 swing is only about plus or minus EUR 15m of PBT GS. FY2027 EPS ranges from EUR 14.4 to 16.2: the stress case is minus 7.5 percent at perhaps 15 percent probability, the bull case +4 percent at 20 percent, and there is about a 65 percent probability of landing within 5 percent of the base case and 90 percent within 10 percent. FY2028 EPS ranges from EUR 15.9 to 18.6 (stress minus 10 percent, bull +5 percent). FY2029 to FY2030 EPS ranges about plus or minus 12 to 15 percent, dominated by Belron's terminal margin, the 2029 refinancing and, at the edge, self-calibration by carmakers.

The skew is down for three reasons. The base case already sits near the top of what Belron's record supports; the risks are correlated; and the downside items are discrete and compounding (a change in the pricing regime, a delay to the social plan, a rate move on EUR 5.5bn of floating debt, a mild winter), while the upside items are incremental and bounded.

Sudden fundamental risks are large but unlikely inside eighteen months. The fundamental risks are: a credit or refinancing shock on Belron's debt stack; a coordinated insurer move or the loss of a major claims-administration role (medium plausibility as gradual erosion, low as a single event; a few percent of EPS directly, but more through the multiple, because calibration is the growth story); rapid self-calibration by carmakers (unlikely before 2030, but large: it would remove about 6 of the 17 points of margin Belron has gained since 2018 and impair Belron's terminal value and listing multiple); Volkswagen moving to agency or worse terms in Belgium (unlikely; Automotive is 7 percent of profit, but D'Ieteren Immo's EUR 411m of property, 80 percent of it leased to Automotive, would follow); and a cyber-attack on a subsidiary that depends on logistics (TVH's 2023 attack cost it market share permanently).

Sudden perception risks are higher than usual now. The perception risks are: a delayed, pulled or under-priced Belron listing (a price below EUR 30bn would mark down the Belron tracker, and Jefferies' downside case, which values Belron at 13.3x EBIT, gives EUR 145 a share); the March 2027 framing; a kitchen sink of charges; read-across from Boyd, Driven, Volkswagen or a US insurer's public calibration policy; and a failed large European IPO. Thin liquidity and a standing family seller amplify each of these risks, and because 81 percent of the stock's variance is idiosyncratic, they land without a sector cushion.

The two drivers are trackable between D'Ieteren's twice-yearly reports. External proxies exist for both: Boyd and Driven; Progressive, Allstate and Travelers; the quarterly NAGS updates; Febiac's monthly Belgian registrations; Belgian union reports; and Belron's bond prices and any Fitch action. The next company event is 10 March 2027, followed by a first-quarter update in late May.

Sector and cyclical risks: distribution is highly cyclical, glass repair is not. Distributors' operating leverage is severe in downturns: from 2008 to 2009, Inchcape's like-for-like revenue fell 20 percent and its EBIT 34 percent. Automotive is the extreme case, with a 24 percent decremental margin in H1 2026, because it combines a cyclical normalisation with a structural plateau and share loss, and it has no precedent of its own for rebuilding its margin through costs. Glass repair is close to GDP-agnostic (UK windscreen claims fell 11 percent when traffic fell 21 percent, and Belron's volume fell 13 percent in 2020 with its EBITDA margin held above 10 percent), but it is sensitive to weather (2012; H1 2024).

The longer-term sector risk is that the market compresses Belron's multiple as calibration penetration plateaus. Growth driven by rising content per job sustains above-market growth until penetration saturates, and the multiple compresses before the earnings slow. The risk window is when penetration approaches its plateau (above 60 percent by FY2028) and a listing invites new investors to price Belron's terminal growth rate. European holding discounts persist through cycles and narrow only on catalysts with a price and a clock.

Trough arithmetic: even a trough multiple on stress-case EPS costs about a quarter of the price, and the Belron stake underwrites the floor. At the ten-year 10th-percentile P/E of 9.3x on today's two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 17.1, the shares are worth EUR 159 (minus 7 percent). At the five-year low of 8.2x, they are worth EUR 140 (minus 18 percent; the 52-week low is EUR 141.8). On stress-case EPS (minus 8 percent) at 8.2x, they are worth about EUR 129 (minus 25 percent). The Belron stake alone covers D'Ieteren's market capitalisation at about 16.6x Belron's EBIT or more; at the 2017 transaction multiple of 13.3x, the stake covers about 72 percent of the market capitalisation and the other assets supply the rest.

Against the market. The market sees a complex, levered holding and prices a wide range of outcomes. The data say the eighteen-month range is narrower than the structure suggests, for two reasons: two-thirds of profit comes from a business with non-discretionary, contracted, indexed demand that has landed within a few percent of expectations for four years, and the portfolio absorbed a 51 percent miss in one segment in H1 2026 with only a 0.3 percent miss at group level. I am more cautious than the market beyond eighteen months, on pricing and refinancing.

Conclusion. The case is simple to state, concentrated in one asset and one customer relationship, correlated in its stresses and self-determined in its share-price risk, which makes it more predictable than its wrapper looks over eighteen months and less predictable than its main asset's record implies beyond that.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The FY2027 EPS cone of EUR 14.4-16.2 around 15.60 (-8%/+4%, 65% within 5%) is narrow for a holding. Two-thirds of profit is non-discretionary, indexed demand that has landed within a few percent for four years, and the drivers have external monthly or quarterly proxies. Against that, the case rests on one asset, one customer type and one price benchmark. Its stresses are correlated with EUR 8.3bn of BB-rated, 77%-floating debt; a coordinated insurer move is a low-probability tail; and the share price carries sudden perception risks (a pulled or under-priced listing, the March framing, a new chief executive's kitchen sink) with 81% idiosyncratic variance, thin float and a standing seller. Between the risk groups (54 and 60), that sits below Banca Generali and just above NKT's concentrated execution risk.

10

Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence: the stock is Bottoming, by the dashboard's rule and by its own history. The dashboard's rule puts the starting phase at Bottoming because the two-year-forward P/E of 9.64x sits against ten-year bands of 9.3x (10th percentile), 10.5x (35th), 11.0x (median), 12.1x (75th) and 13.1x (90th). The stock's own history fits the label. The P/E de-rated from 13.2x in November 2024 (before the recapitalisation and the Automotive downturn) to 9.1x in November and December 2025, made a false start to 11.8x in January 2026 on listing hopes, and fell back to 9.6x in September 2026 after the Automotive miss.

Every other reading is also that of a stock near a bottom, not past it. Technical momentum is D and sell-side momentum F; the revision slope is flat; third parties hold the event clock; the chief executive is changing; and the first guidance under the new chief executive is likely to disappoint in presentation.

Inference: the stock is Bottoming, and the turn-up can be dated rather than left vague. The conditions for "Turning up" are a positive revision slope, a confirmed FY2026 beat, Belron's margin near 24 percent in print and a visible floor under Automotive. On the sequence set out in topics 4 and 7, those conditions arrive between 10 March 2027 (the beat) and the second quarter (the slope), with the September 2027 raise test as confirmation.

The later phases depend on the Belron event and on Belron's deleveraging. "Thesis broadening" needs the listing to be priced and a channel from Belron's value to D'Ieteren's shareholders (a Belron dividend policy or a larger buyback) to be stated: months six to eighteen at the earliest, and more likely 2028. "Reinforcing" belongs to the period when Belron's leverage is below 3x and Belron is distributing cash (2029), beyond this memo's horizon.

The collapse scenarios are unlikely inside eighteen months and would take the stock back to the bottom of its range rather than below it. The collapse scenarios are a listing pulled in a credit crunch, a coordinated insurer move and a Belron recapitalisation. The floor holds because a sum of the parts with Belron at its 2017 multiple, plus the other assets, covers the market capitalisation.

Counter-case. A stock can bottom for a long time when someone else holds the catalyst's clock. The Belron review could run through 2027 without a transaction if credit markets stay hostile, and a holding at a 45 percent discount, with a standing seller and a 39 percent free float, has no natural buyer until the event is dated.

What would change my view. Toward an early "Turning up": a double-digit FY2027 framing in March, or a Belron prospectus with its own targets. Toward "Stalling": Belron's H2 2026 incremental margin below 30 percent, or the Federal Reserve's December rate rise feeding through to a visible increase in Belron's finance costs in H1 2027.

Against the market. The sell-side's Buy ratings imply that the stock is already "Turning up"; the share price and the dashboard say "Bottoming". I side with the share price on timing and with the sell-side on direction.

Conclusion. The stock is Bottoming, with the turn-up most plausibly dated to the second quarter of 2027 after the March air pocket, and thesis broadening depends on the Belron event being priced and paired with a cash channel to D'Ieteren's shareholders.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Bottoming, as computed and as the memo reads it, is right: the two-year-forward P/E is at the 21st-23rd percentile after a de-rating from 13.2x and a false start; technicals are D and sell-side momentum F; and the revision slope has only just flattened. The turn is datable to Q2 2027, after a likely March air pocket, with the September raise test as confirmation, so it is a late-stage Bottoming with a visible route to Turning, not yet Turning. It sits below Indutrade (Bottoming with stronger momentum) and above Solid State's less datable turn.

11

The fair multiple

Evidence: the guideline fair multiple is 10.29x, 7 percent above where the stock trades. Viewforth's guideline for a Bottoming stock is the 30th percentile of its own ten-year two-year-forward P/E history: 10.29x, against 9.64x on 2 November. FactSet's weekly series shows 10.04x, at the 23rd percentile of five years, with a five-year median of 11.17x and a range of 8.19x to 18.65x; the model uses 10.1x. The ten-year median is 11.0x and the 75th percentile 12.1x.

The sector shares the level of D'Ieteren's de-rating but not its day-to-day movement. D'Ieteren's trailing P/E of 9.9x sits at the 21st percentile of its history, and its peers sit at similarly low percentiles of their own histories (the table in topic 8 gives each one, from Auto1's 1st to Inter Cars' 60th).

The asset that carries the value trades at 17 to 20x EBIT. Belron's peers and transactions price it at 17 to 20x EBIT (Boyd and Driven at about 17x; Jefferies' 20x FY2026 EBIT for Belron), with the 2021 private-equity round at 21x and Cary Group at 26x EBITA. Those multiples are not a comparator for the parent's P/E, but they are the reason the parent's sum of the parts sits at EUR 317 against a share price of EUR 171.

My view: 10.29x is the right multiple for the current phase and for the next four months. The reasons the multiple should stay low until March are real: a chief executive not yet in the seat, a listing without a date, a framing event likely to disappoint, 77 percent floating-rate debt in a rising-rate regime, a risk-off market that punishes complexity, and a forming insurer headwind that the sell-side's models do not carry.

The multiple should not stay at the 30th percentile beyond the second quarter of 2027. The growth about to be printed is operational and runs at 13 to 15 percent a year, and the revision slope is turning. The stock's own history says that when Belron compounds cleanly and the rest of the portfolio is not failing (2022 to 2023, mid-2024, January 2026), the market pays 11x to 13x. I therefore treat 10.29x as the fair multiple for the eighteen-month return, and the median 11.0x as the fair multiple for a delivery phase that begins, on this memo's sequence, in the second half of 2027 if the raise test is passed and the listing is priced. The 75th percentile (12.1x) requires both of those plus a stated cash channel. A trough of 9.3x applies to a pulled listing or a coordinated insurer move.

So-what. Each turn of P/E is worth about 10 percent of value, so the multiple is a larger lever than any single earnings judgement in topic 6; the multiple is also the lever with the clearest triggers and the least company control. The right way to hold the valuation is to earn the base-case return at 10.29x and to treat the step to 11.0x as the reward for the March-to-September 2027 sequence, not as the base case.

Counter-case. Car-retail peers at 6 to 7x (Inchcape, Ayvens) show where a mixed group can be priced in a de-rating, and holding discounts of 50 percent (Wendel, Kinnevik) show that a parent's P/E can stay compressed for years whatever its assets are worth. A listed Belron, by giving investors direct access to the asset, could make D'Ieteren less necessary to own and widen its discount (Berenberg's warning) unless D'Ieteren pairs the listing with buybacks.

What would change my view. Upward: an FY2027 framing at double digits or a Belron prospectus, either of which would move the fair multiple to 11.0x immediately. Downward: Belron's leverage stalling above 4x or a Belron recapitalisation, either of which would justify the 10th-percentile multiple.

Against the market. The sell-side's targets (EUR 201 to 270; median EUR 230) are sum-of-the-parts figures at a narrowed discount, not P/E targets. Translated, they imply about 11.5x to 13x FY2028 EPS, which is a delivery-phase multiple applied to a bottoming stock. I apply the bottoming multiple now and the delivery multiple later.

Conclusion. The guideline fair multiple of 10.29x (the 30th percentile) is the right multiple for a bottoming stock with a new chief executive and an undated event, and the stock's own history shows that 11.0x to 12.1x becomes available once the operating growth is printed and the event is priced, which on this memo's sequence is the second half of 2027.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C. I place it in the upper half because both readings lean cheap: the memo's two-year-forward multiple is just above the 20th-percentile cheap line, and the holding discount of 45% sits against a ten-year average of 30%. It stays short of B because part of the cheapness is deserved for a Bottoming stock with a new chief executive, an undated event, family-first governance and junk-rated floating debt at Belron; the memo's own guideline of 10.29x is only 7% above today.

The return is an earnings return with a small multiple kicker and a small dividend.

Dividends of EUR 2.10 for FY2026 and EUR 2.30 for FY2027 (then EUR 2.60 and 2.90) give a 1.2 to 1.4 percent yield on a 15 percent payout ratio. Reading the matrix: the skew favours the shareholder. The correlated stress case at a trough multiple costs about zero to minus 10 percent, because the multiple is already near its floor and the sum of the parts underwrites it. The base case at the median multiple earns about +30 percent, and the Belron event priced and paired with a cash channel earns +40 to 50 percent.

The earnings leg is the dependable part of the return, and the multiple leg is the free option. Two-thirds of the base return comes from a business that has delivered for four years. The probabilities on the sequence in topics 4 and 7 (about 70 percent for the March air pocket, 45 percent for a September raise, and perhaps 60 percent for a listing within eighteen months) put the expected value modestly above the guideline return rather than below it.

Counter-case. The "18-month" column ends on a fixed date, 31 December 2027, which is fourteen months away, not eighteen, so the annualised figure flatters the return. The return also rests on a two-year-forward EPS that the market may not capitalise if FY2029 consensus is being cut at the same time; I expect cuts of 5 to 10 percent to the two-broker FY2029 figure, toward the model's own EUR 19.3. The dividend leg is thin and will not cushion a drawdown.

What would change my view. The matrix row (the multiple) changes with the March and September 2027 events and with the listing's price; the column (EPS) changes with Belron's reported price and mix and with the Automotive floor. A listing at or above EUR 34bn paired with a step-up in buybacks moves the case to the bottom-right cell; a pulled listing combined with a coordinated insurer move moves it to the top-left cell.

Against the market. The sell-side's EUR 230 median target lands in the matrix's 11.0x row (EUR 219 on base EPS, EUR 230 on bull EPS), but the sell-side reaches it by a different road: a narrowed discount. I reach the same value by a dated route and without needing the discount to close, which is a stronger claim.

Conclusion. At the guideline multiple the stock offers about +20 percent to end-2027 and +32 percent to mid-2029, almost all of it from earnings the business has shown it can deliver. A multiple option worth a further 10 to 25 percent can be unlocked by the March-to-September 2027 sequence and the Belron event, against a stress-and-trough downside of about zero to minus 10 percent.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. 20-35% gives B, low in the band; about 21% maps to about 76. I move it up a point because the lower tail is thin: stress EPS at a trough multiple costs about 0 to -10%, underwritten by a sum of the parts, while the median-multiple cell gives +30%. The three-year check of about 11% a year is only ordinary, and the column ends after fourteen months on a two-year-forward EPS that may be cut.

13

Summary conclusion

The conclusion

D'Ieteren is a top-decile asset, Belron, inside a middling wrapper, and the market prices it as the wrapper. The earnings return of about 20 percent to end-2027 does not need the discount to narrow; the Belron event, paired with a cash channel, is the upside.

The investment case over the next twelve to twenty-four months rests on three demonstrated pillars and one undemonstrated one. The first demonstrated pillar is Belron's content-driven, insurer-paid, regulation-mandated growth engine, which is still accelerating (calibration penetration up 6 points in a year, organic growth of 7.3 percent, a margin of 23 to 24 percent and rising) and converts extra revenue to profit at incremental margins of 35 to 45 percent. The second is a deleveraging that has done its heavy lifting (from 5.4x to 4.3x) and now adds a small, steady tailwind. The third is a guidance institution that sets floors and beats them. The undemonstrated pillar is the Automotive cost-out under Belgian consultation, which is small in profit but is the one driver the sell-side disputes.

The earnings path matches consensus in level and beats it in composition. EPS grows 13 to 15 percent a year in FY2027 and FY2028, in line with consensus, and the market has not yet noticed that the source of the growth has changed from financial to operational.

The reasons for the low multiple are mostly behind the stock or dated. The multiple sits at the bottom of its ten-year range because of a 2024 transaction that put the family first, the Automotive collapse, a levered subsidiary, an undated Belron event and a new chief executive.

The risks that could break the case are named, monitorable and correlated, and one event could make the case. The breaking risks are US insurers moving faster than carrier-by-carrier on calibration and NAGS pricing, a relapse in the US consumer combined with a mild winter, a slipping Belgian consultation, and a rise in rates on floating-rate debt. The making event is a Belron listing priced in the mooted range and paired by the new chief executive with a channel from Belron's cash to D'Ieteren's shareholders; the precedents say that pairing is the difference between Investor AB's 12 percent discount and Prosus's 40 percent.

The sequence to watch: 10 March 2027 (the beat and the air pocket), the second quarter of 2027 (the revision turn), the May 2027 annual general meeting (capital allocation), September 2027 (the raise test) and the Belron process throughout.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 66, set by the Rater. A clear net positive change because a mandated, profit-weighted external tailwind at Belron (topic 1, 64) and working self-help and deleveraging (topic 2, 62) reach profits fairly surely, as two years of 13-15% EPS growth on organic operations and a record margin (topic 6, B 77). It sits in the mid-60s rather than the 75s because the four-year growth of about 10.5% is only typical of the Universe, the forces fade after FY2028, and the largest change, the Belron review, acts on the multiple rather than on profits.

Foundations' Robustness: 73, set by the Rater. Robust because the value carrier has the stability Richard prizes: a dominant leader over a fragmented tail, a barrier rising with every model year, non-discretionary insurer-paid and mandated demand, and margins that have landed within a few percent of expectations for four years, plus PHE's and TVH's niche leadership (topic 3, 68), under a group guidance institution that sets floors and beats them (topic 4, 66). It is held below the high 70s because the moat sits in one asset held through a levered, junk-rated, family-first wrapper with a low reported return, and the non-Belron units have missed.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 66, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits a cause-for-concern clearing in a high-quality business (Belron's compounding engine beneath an Automotive collapse, the 2024 governance episode and a levered subsidiary), with an earnings step-up underneath. The fit is clear in kind. It is not crisp because the quality is blurred by the holding wrapper and two concerns are not yet cleared in the business: Automotive's reset still awaits a Belgian social plan, and nothing yet carries Belron's value to D'Ieteren's shareholders. That is close to Richard's 65-75 for a major concern clearing, at the lower end for those current problems; the March timing and price are left to topics 7 and 12.

Case Riskiness: 57, set by the Rater. Moderate because the 18-month earnings cone is narrow and trackable, guidance is conservative and the multiple already sits low in its range (topic 9, 56), which bounds the downside. The risk is not mere paper cuts, though: the drivers concentrate in one asset and one customer type, the stresses are correlated with junk-rated floating debt, and a new chief executive succeeding a successful ten-year incumbent faces a listing event others control, without a sector cushion.

End notes.

Basis of the figures

Money is in EUR millions unless stated. PBT GS is adjusted profit before tax, group share, the company's guided line. EPS is on the brokers' adjusted basis: FY2025 EPS of EUR 12.95 equals PBT GS x 0.72 / about 53.1m shares. The share price is EUR 171.3 (29 October 2026); the model's total shareholder return is struck at EUR 170.90 (28 October 2026). Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 1 (the Viewforth base case), which the second and third analysis rounds built and tested; this memo changes no model input.

Why the memo uses the group-share basis, not FactSet's consolidated lines

FactSet's consolidated perimeter (Automotive, PHE and Moleskine) shows EUR 8.0bn of revenue and EUR 392m of EBIT. Belron (50.3 percent owned), the business that carries the value, and TVH (40 percent owned) are equity-accounted, so they appear only below the operating line. FactSet's consolidated revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, operating margin and return on invested capital therefore describe neither the assets nor the holding.

Two corrections to the model's one-page summary

The model summary's FY2026 EPS of EUR 9.22 is a tax artefact, not a view. The summary shows FY2026 EPS of EUR 9.22, "minus 31 percent against consensus". FY2026 is the one forecast year that contains a reported half, and the model carried H1 2026's consolidated tax charge alongside 28 percent of an H2 base. The Analyst's cross-check EPS of EUR 13.63 is correct, and the memo uses it. The Financial Analyst should set FY2026's tax charge at 28 percent of the year's pre-tax profit (about EUR 278m on EUR 992m), overriding the reported H1 2026 contribution, so that FY2026 net income reads about EUR 714m and EPS about EUR 13.6.

The model's equity free cash flow and year-end net cash are unusable for this company. The model's equity free cash flow (EUR 441m to 1,050m) is overstated because its net-financial-items line carries equity-accounted profit that is not cash. The Analyst's free cash flow to D'Ieteren (EUR 292m to 597m) is the right series, and the memo uses it. The Financial Analyst should label the model's equity free cash flow and year-end net cash as not usable for this company, or replace them with the Analyst's cross-check figures.

Neither fault affects the total shareholder return in the summary, because that return is built from EPS, the multiple and the dividend.

Sources and grades

Default charts and tables are from FactSet, the Viewforth Master Dashboard and the model's one-page summary, as noted under each. Drawn charts take their figures from the memo. Grades are filled from the Rater's scores; each topic's score and its reason are the Rater's own words.

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • FY2025 earnings per share: 12.95 on the brokers' basis against 7.62 on our model's basis (+69.9%).

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Holdings in associates: 1,347.0, 13.5% of market capitalisation.
  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
